findings.claim: Using OpenSecrets data, the Election Law Blog reported that Bloomberg gave $64.3 million in the 2024 cycle, nearly all to Democrats, making him the largest donor on that side. Forbes records that he was mayor of New York from 2002 to 2013 and owns 88% of Bloomberg LP.

The New York Times reported in October 2026 that Bloomberg had given about $80 million to Democratic candidates and groups in September and October 2026, including $24 million to Everytown and $16 million to House Majority PAC. The figures came from his team before the filings were due.

Bloomberg put about $1.09 billion of his own money into his 2020 presidential campaign. A complaint said the campaign’s $18 million transfer to the DNC broke contribution limits. In May 2023 the FEC dismissed it as a matter of prosecutorial discretion, citing no sign of intent to get around the limits.

In May 2020 the SEC found that Bloomberg Tradebook, then a broker unit, misled customers about an undisclosed order-routing arrangement used from 2010 to 2018. It was censured and paid a $5 million penalty, without admitting or denying the findings.

In January 2023 Bloomberg Finance paid a $5 million SEC penalty. The SEC said that from 2016 to 2022 it did not tell BVAL customers that some bond valuations could rest on a single input such as one broker quote. It settled without admitting or denying the findings.

The EEOC sued Bloomberg L.P. in 2007, alleging a pattern of discrimination against pregnant employees. In August 2011 a federal judge dismissed the pattern-or-practice claim, finding the evidence insufficient; individual claims could proceed. Bloomberg was not named personally.

Former saleswoman Sekiko Sakai Garrison sued Bloomberg personally and his company over alleged harassment and pregnancy discrimination in 1995, over 25 years ago. He denied it under oath and settled confidentially. In 2020 he let three women out of NDAs over his alleged comments and ended such agreements.

In May 2025 a Massachusetts jury found that Bloomberg’s 2020 campaign broke an oral promise of work through November 2020 to field organizer Nygel O’Bannon; the judgment was later set at about $53,750. Both sides appealed. In a related state case, Doty, a claim against the campaign is pending.

In June 2026 a federal judge in Massachusetts let a former campaign worker pursue a breach-of-contract claim against Bloomberg personally and his campaign over the promised jobs. The case is pending; he denies making the promise. A state judge had dismissed him personally from the Doty case in March 2026.

Authors led by Mike Huckabee allege that Bloomberg trained its BloombergGPT model on their copyrighted books without permission. In November 2025 a federal judge in New York denied Bloomberg’s motion to dismiss, saying fair use needs a factual record. The case is pending; nothing has been decided on the merits.
The Bloomberg Family Foundation reported charitable disbursements of about $1.47 billion in fiscal 2024 and $1.42 billion in 2023, according to its Form 990-PF filings.

The Chronicle of Philanthropy ranked Bloomberg the largest US donor of 2025, with $4.3 billion, personally and through Bloomberg Philanthropies, and $25.4 billion over his lifetime. The Chronicle counts multiyear gifts in the year announced, so this is not a disbursed total.

politics.reason: Gave $64.3 million in the 2024 cycle, nearly all to Democrats, the largest donor on that side by OpenSecrets data, and about $80 million in autumn 2026 by his team’s account. Put about $1.09 billion into his 2020 presidential run; the FEC dismissed a complaint over an $18 million transfer to the DNC. Mayor of New York from 2002 to 2013 and owner of 88% of Bloomberg LP, a major news organisation.

social.reason: A Massachusetts jury found in 2025 that his 2020 campaign broke a promise of work to a field organizer; the verdict is on appeal. The SEC found that Bloomberg units misled customers on order routing (2020) and bond valuations (2023), settled without admission. An EEOC pattern-of-pregnancy-bias claim against Bloomberg L.P. was dismissed in 2011. In 2020 he released three women from NDAs over his alleged comments.

legal.reason: Bloomberg was a named defendant in a 1990s harassment and pregnancy-discrimination suit that he settled confidentially, denying the claims. At company level, Bloomberg units paid $5 million SEC penalties in 2020 and 2023 without admitting the findings, and the EEOC’s pattern-of-discrimination claim was dismissed in 2011. The FEC dismissed a complaint about his campaign’s transfer to the DNC in 2023. No penalty against him personally was found.

unresolved.reason: Since June 2026 a federal court in Massachusetts has let a former campaign worker pursue a contract claim against Bloomberg personally; he denies making the promise. Related claims against his 2020 campaign, including an appealed jury verdict, are pending. A copyright suit over training BloombergGPT on authors’ books is pending against Bloomberg L.P. after dismissal was denied in 2025.

proposal.counterweights: The Bloomberg Family Foundation reported about $1.47 billion in charitable disbursements in 2024 (Form 990-PF). The Chronicle of Philanthropy counted $4.3 billion given or committed in 2025, the most of any US donor.
proposal.rationale: Legal 0 to 2: R3, a personal settlement with no penalty (Garrison suit), as for Ellison 2005; company SEC penalties alone are 1. Unresolved 0 to 3: R6, he is a named defendant in a pending federal contract suit (amNY, July 2026; single source). Social 1 to 2: company-level labour verdict and SEC findings. Politics stays 3.
